items.factual_review: Oscar Wilde authored The Picture of Dorian Gray. Project Gutenberg's opening identifies Basil Hallward as the artist beside the portrait and Lord Henry as his interlocutor; Dorian is the subject and character. The public Harvard University Press/JSTOR description and textual-introduction preview support the July 1890 magazine appearance, Wilde's later enlargement for book publication, and Nicholas Frankel's edition based on a typescript with Wilde's emendations. The article does not turn publisher speculation about Wilde's preferred version into a unique final authorial intention or collapse the editor, fictional artist, and author.
items.option_review: Bram Stoker, Arthur Conan Doyle, and Robert Louis Stevenson are distinct authors and not defensible answers to this named-work authorship stem. Basil Hallward is the fictional painter, not an alternative literary author.

items.pedagogy_review: The short dialogue-and-edition comparison is concrete and optional. It distinguishes character speech from author belief and asks the reader to identify an edition without asserting a measured learning result.

items.factual_review: Library of America identifies Herman Melville as author of Moby-Dick, dates the novel 1851, names Ahab's hunt of the white whale, describes Ishmael's reflections, and credits G. Thomas Tanselle as editor of its volume. Project Gutenberg chapter I has the narrator ask to be called Ishmael, mention little or no money, and express a wish to go to sea. The article keeps narrator, captain, author, and later editor distinct and avoids literal autobiography or medical diagnosis.
items.option_review: Jack London, Jules Verne, and Joseph Conrad are separate writers and not defensible answers to this named-work authorship stem; Captain Ahab and Ishmael are characters, not competing authors.
items.source_review: Both exact final URLs opened with relevant text: Library of America lines 22–24 and 43–50; Project Gutenberg chapter I lines 542–545. These are an edition description and a modern digital transcription, not inspection of a first edition or evidence of a clinical condition. items.pedagogy_review: The optional passage annotation separates events, narration, and reflection, and the caution about treating nineteenth-century literary passages as current biology is appropriately framed without a measured learning claim.
